opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I tend to start by asking what kind of normative standard we're actually dealing with, because I think a lot of alignment work treats every norm as a preference to maximize, and that hides important distinctions.

Some standards are rules or conventions that a community has settled on: traffic laws, professional codes, the informal norms of a workplace. Others are more open-ended, like being honest or being fair, and they depend heavily on context and interpretation. Still others are role-specific. What we expect from a medical assistant differs from what we expect from a coding assistant or a negotiating agent acting for someone. So before picking a method, I want to know whose standards these are, where they come from, and what gives them authority.

That shapes the method. If the norms are reasonably explicit and agreed on, I'm drawn to approaches where the system represents them in a structured, inspectable way. That might mean something like a probabilistic program or a formal specification that the system reasons over, rather than hoping the right behavior falls out of a reward signal. The benefit is that you can audit it, contest it, and revise it when the community's understanding changes.

When the norms are implicit, which is most of the time, I think the system has to infer them. A lot of my work has been on Bayesian inverse planning, modeling people as boundedly rational agents with goals and then inferring what they want or what rules they follow from what they do and say. You can extend that to norms: watch how a group behaves, notice which actions get sanctioned and which are just never taken, and infer the shared rules that explain it. Crucially, the system should keep its uncertainty about those inferences, so it can be cautious or ask when it isn't sure, rather than confidently optimizing a misread objective.

Underneath all of this is a more philosophical commitment. I'm skeptical of the idea that alignment means aggregating everyone's preferences into one utility function and maximizing it. Human normativity doesn't really work that way. It's closer to a contractualist picture, where norms are what people could reasonably agree to, given that they have different values and need to live together. So I'd rather build systems that act within the bounds of what the relevant stakeholders would endorse than systems that try to compute some global good on everyone's behalf.

In practice, then, I'm choosing methods based on a few criteria. Does the approach respect the actual structure of the norm? Can the system represent and act on its uncertainty? Is the result legible enough for people to hold it accountable? And does it leave room for the norms themselves to be contested and to change? Methods that score well on those tend to be more modular and model-based than pure end-to-end training. I don't think that means abandoning learning, but I want learning to serve an explicit model of what the system is trying to respect.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I try not to start with the method at all. I start with the question of what we actually mean by "normative standards," because that phrase is doing a lot of work, and the method you pick depends enormously on how you unpack it.

A lot of alignment work today treats norms as if they're just preferences in disguise. You collect human judgments, you fit a reward model, you optimize against it, and the hope is that whatever "the norms" are, they'll come out in the wash. And that approach has had real success. But I think it quietly conflates several different things. There's what people happen to want, there's what they'd endorse on reflection, there's what a community has agreed to as a shared rule, and there's what's actually morally required. Those come apart all the time, and a system that's only tracking the first one will behave badly precisely in the cases that matter most.

So the first thing I ask is: what kind of norm is this, and where does its authority come from? Some norms are more like conventions or contracts. "Don't share this user's data with that user." Those are explicit, they're legible, and I think they should be represented explicitly. You want the system to be able to state the rule, reason about whether a situation falls under it, and ideally explain its interpretation. For that, I lean toward structured, often symbolic or probabilistic-programming style representations, because you can inspect them, you can verify them to some degree, and you can revise them when the community changes its mind. Burying a rule like that inside the weights of a reward model feels like exactly the wrong tool.

Other norms are much more tacit and contextual. What counts as rude, what counts as helpful, when a white lie is fine. Those are hard to write down, and here learning from human behavior and feedback is really the only game in town. But even then, I think you want the learning to be structured by a model of why people are behaving the way they are. Humans aren't just emitting approval signals. They're acting on beliefs and goals and their own understanding of the norms, and they make mistakes. If you model that generatively, as inverse planning or theory-of-mind inference, you get something much more robust than treating every thumbs-up as ground truth.

The second thing I weigh heavily is contestability. Whatever method I choose, I want it to be possible for people to disagree with the result and have that disagreement land somewhere. Norms in human societies are maintained through ongoing negotiation. We argue about them, we revise them, we carve out exceptions. If a system's normative behavior is a frozen artifact of a training run that nobody can audit, we've effectively taken that negotiation away from people. So I'm drawn to approaches where the normative content lives somewhere that can be read, challenged, and amended, even if the underlying capabilities are learned.

And the third thing, which I think gets underrated, is being honest about uncertainty. We don't have moral consensus, and we don't have full access to our own values. So I'd rather build systems that represent normative uncertainty explicitly and act cautiously under it, deferring, asking, or choosing options that are acceptable across a range of plausible standards, than systems that commit confidently to one aggregated answer. That's a methodological choice too. It pushes you toward Bayesian and decision-theoretic framings rather than pure optimization.

So in practice it ends up being a pluralist toolkit. Explicit representation where norms are explicit, model-based learning where they're tacit, and uncertainty-aware decision-making layered over both. The common thread is that I don't want the method to decide the metaethics for me by accident. I'd rather make those commitments visible, even if it's messier.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start by asking what kind of normative standard you’re trying to get the system to comply with. Is it a rule that we can state explicitly and check, or is it something like fairness or helpfulness, where people disagree about what it means in context? Those call for different methods.

If you have a clear constraint, you might be able to enforce it through the design of the system, or use formal methods to verify that certain actions are ruled out. If the standard depends on context and judgment, then learning from human feedback may be useful. But that raises a further question: whose feedback, and how do we handle disagreement?

So I wouldn’t treat this as simply choosing the best technical alignment method. The choice of method already makes assumptions about where normative authority comes from. I’d want to make those assumptions explicit, and then choose a combination of methods that lets us check compliance, understand failures, and revise the system when our understanding of the standard changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to start by asking what the normative standard actually is, and who gets to determine it, before choosing a technical method. Are we talking about complying with a law, respecting someone’s preferences, or navigating a moral disagreement? Those are different problems, and I wouldn’t expect one approach to solve all of them.

If a requirement is clear and can be specified precisely, then explicit constraints or formal verification might be appropriate. If the system needs to interpret context or understand what people want, then learning from feedback or inferring preferences might be more useful. But learning what people tend to approve of isn’t automatically the same as learning what’s right.

So I’d look for a combination of methods, guided by the particular setting. And I’d want the system to represent uncertainty about the relevant norms—to ask for clarification, defer to appropriate human judgment, and remain open to correction. The aim shouldn’t just be to produce behavior that looks compliant on a benchmark, but to have a process through which we can understand and contest how those standards are being applied.
